articles.title: Trump calls Ukraine attack on Russian oil refineries 'a disgrace', irks Zelenskyy
articles.summary: European leaders are preparing to reassure Ukraine of their continued support as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets them in Brussels, with Kyiv facing
articles.body: European leaders are preparing to reassure Ukraine of their continued support as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets them in Brussels, with Kyiv facing intensifying Russian attacks, uncertainty over US assistance and mounting financial needs ahead of winter.The summit comes amid fresh tensions between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Ukraine's fresh attacks on Russian oil refineries and accused Kyiv of driving up global energy prices. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy infrastructure, an announcement that took Zelenskyy by surprise last weekend.Trump reiterated his criticism after Ukraine struck a refinery southeast of Moscow that helps supply the Russian capital."All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.The Ukrainian president, meanwhile, said there was little indication that Moscow was ready to end the war and warned that Kyiv needed to prepare for the coming winter."We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter," Zelenskyy said as he arrived at the summit."The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defence and funding," he said, adding that he would discuss Ukraine's requirements for the rest of this year and 2027.Ukraine seeks billions in military aidFinancial and military assistance is expected to feature prominently in discussions as Kyiv faces a substantial funding shortfall. Zelenskyy told Reuters earlier this month that Ukraine had agreed on a plan with European partners to cover a $27 billion deficit in military spending this year, allowing it to order drones needed to sustain its war effort into early 2027.However, finance minister Sergii Marchenko recently said Ukraine still faced an unfunded budget gap of $32.6 billion for next year. That figure does not include an estimated $40 billion in direct military supplies expected from allies.Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten expressed disappointment at the level of new financial commitments made by European countries, while indicating that further military assistance could be announced."I am unhappy with the number of countries that have been willing to pledge new financial support to Ukraine. But we will see several countries pledging more military support soon," Jetten said.He added that the discussions would focus on helping Ukraine navigate the diplomatic challenges and withstand the winter."Today will be more about talking to Zelenskyy about how to deal with the complex diplomatic situation that has arisen and how to survive the winter."Jetten also criticised Trump's language towards Ukraine, arguing that Washington had a stake in helping Kyiv defend itself."This is not the right language. It is also in the interest of Trump to defend Ukraine in this war," he said when asked about the US president's latest remarks.Russian attacks deepen Ukraine's winter concernsRussian continues to target Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, increasing concerns over the country's ability to maintain electricity supplies as temperatures fall.Drone attacks on Kharkiv killed three people, according to local authorities. Strikes in the Volyn region, which borders Poland, left 370,000 people without electricity, while emergency power cuts were introduced in Kyiv during Russian attacks, private energy provider DTEK said on X.Russia, however, has played down the impact of Ukraine's attacks on its oil infrastructure. President Vladimir Putin said the strikes had caused "nothing particularly significant".Moscow has also placed local assets belonging to French, German, Swedish and Dutch companies under temporary management, a move described as retaliation for the European Union's support for Ukraine.The dispute over energy infrastructure has added another complication for European leaders, who are already grappling with higher energy prices following the war involving Iran. EU leaders criticised Trump's proposed arrangement concerning diesel supplies, while divisions over the energy crisis emerged among member states at the summit on Thursday.Belgian prime minister Bart De Wever warned that Ukraine's funding needs would remain substantial even with the support already pledged by Europe.Zelenskyy, he said, "will probably look everybody straight in the eye and say, thank you for the 90 billion, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing."De Wever said European governments would need to decide whether they were prepared to sustain their commitments."So are you, as a European family, still willing, ready and able to put your money where your mouths are and support Ukraine and keep Ukrainian society and Ukrainian defence up and running?" he said.Trump weighs sanctions relief as tensions growThe uncertainty surrounding US support extends beyond Trump's criticism of Ukraine's military strategy. A US official said on Wednesday that the administration was considering easing sanctions on vessels belonging to the so-called shadow fleet, which has transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia.The possibility of sanctions relief has added to European concerns over Washington's approach to Moscow, particularly as Ukraine continues to rely on Western intelligence, weapons and financial assistance.With Russian attacks continuing and Ukraine preparing for another winter of war, Zelenskyy's Brussels visit is expected to focus on securing the support needed to sustain the country's defence and keep essential services running into 2027.You use AI every day. articles.title: FBI, Philly police dig up Horsch backyard at home tied to 7 missing women in possible serial killer probe
articles.summary: RC Horsch's Philadelphia home is being excavated again as FBI investigators probe links to seven missing women and disturbing video evidence.
articles.body: Police and the FBI have returned to dig up the backyard of a Philadelphia home as part of an ongoing investigation into a potential serial killer that has already turned up apparent "snuff" films, ash-filled urns and evidence linked to at least seven missing women. Images show an excavator in the backyard as police in protective gear continue to come and go from the property this week. They've set up tents in the backyard and out front and covered parts of the lawn in tarps. Investigators could be seen wearing various levels of safety equipment, including face masks, hazmat suits, rubber gloves, protective sleeves and booties. One crime scene investigator was seen wearing what appeared to be a chemical-spraying backpack as she entered the property. A crime scene photographer also came and went Wednesday. Joseph Giacalone, a retired NYPD cold case sergeant and adjunct professor at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice, said the scale of the investigation stands out to him. "The sheer number of crime scene technicians that are going in and out of this house — usually you try to keep it to a minimum because you don't want people trampling on things and stuff like that," he told Fox News Digital. "I just think that there's so many different nooks and crannies that they have to cover that they need this many people. So, I mean, we're not talking three or four, we're talking 10, 12, or 14 people going in and out of this place at one time." WATCH: FBI's Evidence Response Team continues investigation at the home of Eugene Horsch Police have repeatedly visited the home in recent weeks, carrying out boxes of evidence earlier this month, including one marked "glass vials." A Philadelphia Police Department spokesperson declined to go into specifics about the continued searches Thursday, citing the active and ongoing investigation. PHILLY SERIAL KILLER PROBE COULD EXPOSE LARGER NETWORK BEHIND APPARENT 'SNUFF' FILMS, EXPERT SAYS "Investigators continue to examine evidence and pursue all available leads," she told Fox News Digital. "At this time, we are unable to provide specific details regarding investigative activities at the property, any potential findings, or the status of efforts to authenticate the previously recovered images and videos." Raymond "RC" Horsch, a producer of BDSM-themed pornography and books, died last year at 82. However, police searched his former home after arresting his 44-year-old son Eugene Horsch in June. The younger Horsch was arrested in a car alongside a woman carrying an ID belonging to one of the seven missing women now linked to the investigation. They also found a drum of chemicals hooked up to the house's water system. "Investigations predicated on forensic evidence can sometimes result in repeated trips back to a crime scene," said James Gagliano, a retired FBI supervisory agent and Fox News contributor. "You find something that initiates a search into a different area. We saw how early release of a crime scene in Tucson led to so many questions. They won’t make that mistake here." Philadelphia police identified Maribel Fresses, 26, who vanished in 2018, and Gabrielle Amarando, 27, earlier in the investigation. During Eugene Horsch's arrest, the woman with him had an ID for Blair Tonzelli, 38, who was last seen in Philadelphia in February 2023, police told Fox News Digital in September. The other is Nicole "Nikki" Fusaro, 34, according to CBS' Philadelphia affiliate, citing local police sources. She was 27 when she vanished near the intersection of Kensington and Allegheny Avenue in July 2019. articles.title: In 2016, a Canadian diver hunting sea cucumbers spotted a giant metal “bagel” underwater; the Navy ruled out a bomb but its origin remained unknown
articles.summary: In 2016, diver Sean Smyrichinsky discovered a man-made object resembling a giant bagel off the coast of British Columbia. Investigations revealed its connection to a U.S. bomber incident, but its origin remains unidentified. The Canadian Navy confirmed it posed no threat, yet the mystery continues.
articles.body: Banks Island lies off British Columbia’s North Coast, near Haida Gwaii, where the water is cold and the seabed is rocky. Commercial divers work this coast for seafood, and giant red sea cucumbers are one of the species they harvest. In October 2016, diver Sean Smyrichinsky was separated from his boat during an expedition, and on the seabed he spotted a large, unusual object. In an early November 2016 interview with CBC Radio’s Daybreak North, Sean Smyrichinsky described his discovery. The news about it quickly spread all over Canada and abroad. The shape was clearly man-made but had no clear function. Smyrichinsky mentioned his discovery to other fishermen, and one of them linked the object to an American bomber that had crashed in the area many years earlier. What began as a diver’s discovery became an investigation by the RCMP and the Royal Canadian Navy. This investigation answered one question, but kept the other open.Sean Smyrichinsky’s October 31, 2016 report to the Canadian Armed ForcesCTV News reported that Smyrichinsky contacted the Canadian Armed Forces on October 31, 2016, about an object he spotted approximately 80 kilometres from Prince Rupert. Looking down from above, he first thought it was a big round rock, but he later concluded that it was man-made and far too big for any small boat to have brought there. Radio-Canada International quoted his description of a bagel cut into two pieces, with ball-shaped fittings molded around it that were larger than basketballs. After the fisherman’s suggestion, he searched online for images of the Mark IV bomb, and the resemblance became obvious to him.The B-36 that jettisoned a Mark IV bomb on February 13, 1950The Black Vault’s online reading room hosts the Department of Defense report Narrative Summaries of Accidents Involving US Nuclear Weapons, 1950-1980, which documents the bomber incident. Aviation Safety Network lists the B-36 as flying from Eielson Air Force Base to Carswell Air Force Base and notes that a dummy core was inserted in the bomb it carried, while Legion Magazine described the mission as a planned 24-hour non-stop flight with simulated bomb runs over California before continuing to Texas. After six hours of flight, serious technical problems forced the crew to shut down three engines at 12,000 feet, and icing prevented the aircraft from flying level. The plane flew over the Pacific and dropped the weapon from 8,000 feet. The summary said that only high explosive material exploded, after which the aircraft was flown over Princess Royal Island, and the crew parachuted.The crew’s survival and the wreckage found in 1953 on MountAtomic Archive’s list of broken arrow accidents gives the bomb’s weight as 10,800 pounds, and the records indicated that the bomb carried a lead-filled dummy capsule rather than a plutonium core, so a nuclear explosion was not possible. History.com said that the bomber had 17 crew members, 12 of whom were recovered alive while five did not survive. The bomber continued to fly without its crew and crashed near Mount Kologet in northern British Columbia. B.C. Magazine reported that the Royal Canadian Air Force launched Operation Brix to find the missing airmen. Legion Magazine reported that the Royal Canadian Air Force spotted the wreckage in 1953 while searching for another missing aircraft, and that no radiation was found. ScienceAlert put the crash site on Mount Kologet about 300 kilometres from where the bomb was jettisoned.HMCS Yellowknife’s November 22 survey south of Prince RupertThe Northern View reported that the navy sent HMCS Yellowknife to the area on November 22, with Smyrichinsky aboard to help locate the object. The team used sonar, a remotely operated vehicle and dive teams in the search. The Canadian Press reported that the object lay under 8 metres of water, measured 5.5 metres long and 1 metre high, and was painted yellow.The navy announced that the discovered object was not unexploded military ordnance and did not pose any threat to nearby communities. The object was found underwater, but the available sources do not establish its origin or confirm that it was part of an industrial machine. The statement released by the navy did not give any details about the machine or its owner, and Radio-Canada International added that the Canadian Armed Forces were seeking help from the public in identifying the object.How the sea cucumber dive fishery works in British ColumbiaSmyrichinsky was in these waters because of a regulated fishery. Fisheries and Oceans Canada describes the giant red sea cucumber, Apostichopus californicus, in Science Advisory Report 2022/051 as the subject of a commercial dive fishery with 85 licences. As the life history of the species is not well known, four Experimental Fishing Areas were established in 1998 to assess the impacts of harvesting on the population density of sea cucumbers. The report proposed a limit reference point of 0.029 sea cucumbers per square metre of sea cucumber habitat and an upper stock reference level of 0.038 sea cucumbers per square metre for the commercial fishery. The department’s management plan summary adds that this is the only sea cucumber species harvested commercially in the province. It also adds that the vessels in the fishery have licenses for other dive fisheries, such as geoduck and sea urchin. Such activity may involve going through the seabed that few others venture to, and this could be why the unknown object was spotted.Why the navy’s findings left the object’s origin unresolvedThe navy’s findings settled the safety question but not the question of origin. They ruled out unexploded military ammunition, and CBC reported that the object was likely industrial machinery, yet none of the sources consulted prove where it came from. The dummy bomb was probably left on the seabed near where the crew dropped it, and Legion Magazine noted that the 2016 claim was dismissed as too far from that site. The Department of Defense report defines jettisoning as a nuclear weapons accident, so the 1950 case is included in its list of 32 accidents. That file was reopened more than six decades after the accident.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Don't try to bulldoze another Constitutional Amendment Bill': Kharge writes to PM Modi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Friday wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the delay in proroguing the Monsoon Session of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Friday wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the delay in proroguing the Monsoon Session of Parliament, which ended in August, describing the situation as “unprecedented”.Urging PM Modi not to “bulldoze” another “far-reaching” Constitutional Amendment Bill, Kharge reiterated his demand for an all-party meeting to discuss the government’s proposals in detail before they are finalised for consideration in Parliament."It has already been 64 days since the Monsoon Session of Parliament was adjourned sine die on August 13 and both Houses of Parliament are yet to be prorogued. This scenario is unprecedented," Kharge said in his letter, which Congress MP Jairam Ramesh shared on X.The Rajya Sabha leader of opposition recalled writing to the prime minister on April 11, seeking an all-party meeting before the government introduced the Constitutional Amendment Bill on Delimitation, which subsequently failed to pass in the Lok Sabha.“You may kindly recall that I had written to you on April 11 to convene an all-party meeting before bringing any Constitutional Amendment Bill on Delimitation. You did not do so. Thereafter, you made the bills public on the late evening of April 14 and convened a special session on April 16. The Constitutional Amendment Bill on Delimitation failed to muster the necessary two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha on April 17 by a decisive margin,” Kharge said.“Thereafter, on July 16 and August 27, I wrote to you again, reiterating our request for an all-party meeting. I am now making this request for the fourth time. All political parties must be given sufficient time to deliberate among themselves, with each other and with all other stakeholders. Please do not once again try to bulldoze a far-reaching Constitutional Amendment Bill through Parliament, as you attempted earlier, only for it to meet its well-deserved fate,” he added.The Monsoon Session of Parliament began on July 20 and concluded as scheduled on August 13. However, proceedings were repeatedly disrupted over issues including the alleged theft of offerings at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya, the NEET paper leak and allegations of police excesses against NEET protesters in Delhi.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Black ink on Tagore: The fight over Bangladesh's identity
articles.summary: The recent defacement of Rabindranath Tagore's portrait in Dhaka has sparked intense debate around Bangladesh's identity and cultural heritage, highlighting the ongoing clash between secularism and religious nationalism.
articles.body: "Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls."More than a century after Rabindranath Tagore penned these lines in Gitanjali, Marzia Khandaker Rimi, a senior leader of Bangladesh's Rashtra Sanglap Forum, smeared black ink across his portrait in Dhaka, declaring that the poet was Indian and his image should be erased. Clearly, domestic as well as international walls exist, and going by the evidence, they may be hardening further, with prominent leaders of the July uprising expressing concern over growing Jamaat influence in the country.The Rashtra Sanglap Forum emerged after Bangladesh's July 2024 uprising. On October 10, Rimi joined others outside Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy to protest what she called "Indian aggression". She also alleged that Tagore mistreated Muslims while managing his family's estates. Rimi was among four people subsequently arrested, including another leader of the forum, ANM Ayas. The incident has reopened old faultlines over what Tagore means to Bangladesh.On October 11, Nurul Haque Nur, Bangladesh's state minister for expatriates' welfare and overseas employment, described the defacement as a "communal Jamaati misdeed". The prime minister's political assistant, Rashed Khan, went further. He accused Jamaat of orchestrating the defacement and alleged that an adviser to its chief had financed materials used by the protesters.Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami assistant secretary general Ahsanul Mahboob Zubair demanded the withdrawal of the case and the immediate release of all four accused. He described the incident leading to their arrest as trivial and alleged that sections of the administration were using such cases to harass forces associated with the July uprising. At an October 14 court hearing, following a heated exchange, bail was rejected and the accused were sent to jail.The portrait that triggered the controversy was one of ten commissioned by Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) for a footpath beautification project. The others included Kazi Nazrul Islam, Satyajit Ray, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and Zainul Abedin, the celebrated Bangladeshi artist who had defended Tagore during the East Pakistan era. On October 13, the corporation added portraits of Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, a pioneer of women's education, and poets Jibanananda Das and Jasimuddin. It removed the portrait of singer and journalist Sanjib Choudhury.The attack itself was aimed at the man who wrote Amar Sonar Bangla, Bangladesh's national anthem. Writer and journalist Amin Al Rashid, who researches the life and work of Jibanananda Das, sees the incident as part of a broader political development since the July 2024 uprising. He points to what he describes as attacks on Bangladesh's Liberation War legacy, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and the Constitution, alongside the growing influence of religious extremism."Turning a poet who died before India and Pakistan even came into existence into a villain in today's Bangladesh suggests a far-reaching political agenda," he told TOI.Rashid questions whether the attack can be explained simply as opposition to India. Those involved, he notes, would themselves have sung Tagore's Amar Sonar Bangla at school assemblies and studied his poems and stories.Concerns about Bangladesh's political direction have also been voiced by Mahfuz Alam, a prominent leader of the July 2024 uprising and former adviser to Muhammad Yunus's interim government. In a Facebook post on October 15, Alam warned that the country had boarded the train of far-right politics. Alam also accused sections of secular civil society of aligning with Jamaat-e-Islami and its student wing, Islami Chhatra Shibir, in opposition to the BNP, warning that they would eventually pay a political price for it. His remarks concerned Bangladesh's broader political trajectory rather than the Tagore incident specifically.Not the first attack on a cultural symbolThe Dhaka incident was not the first time Tagore's image had been blackened in Bangladesh in recent years. In April 2025, a mural of the poet at Kumarkhali in Kushtia district was found defaced with black paint. It was subsequently restored by local authorities. Two months later, another controversy erupted at a site associated with Tagore. On June 10, 2025, a crowd stormed the Rabindra Kacharibari complex at Shahjadpur in Sirajganj district, damaging an auditorium, doors and windows.A more direct attack on a cultural institution occurred in December 2025. In the early hours of December 19, a mob stormed Chhayanaut's cultural complex in Dhaka's Dhanmondi, ransacking offices and classrooms, destroying musical instruments and books, and setting parts of the premises on fire. The attack occurred amid unrest following the death of political activist Sharif Osman Hadi. Some witnesses reported that attackers accused Chhayanaut of promoting Indian culture and argued that it had no place in Bangladesh.The hostility towards Tagore has surfaced beyond Dhaka as well. On October 11, a day after the Segunbagicha incident, Hasibul Islam Maruf, president of the Chhatra Dal unit at Bandherhat Abdul Malek Ukil Degree College in Noakhali, posted a photograph on Facebook showing Tagore's image beneath his feet. The district leadership of Chhatra Dal, the student wing of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, issued him a show-cause notice and expelled him from his organisational position on October 13.A division older than BangladeshTagore's legacy has long been contested, with many of his alleged actions and omissions coming under scrutiny. In 1905, Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal. Tagore opposed the division, joined the Swadeshi movement and composed Amar Sonar Bangla during the campaign. But many Muslims in eastern Bengal welcomed the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, believing it could improve their educational, administrative and political opportunities.Historian Semanti Ghosh examines these competing aspirations in Different Nationalisms: Bengal, 1905–1947 (Oxford University Press, 2016). She argues that Muslim support for partition cannot simply be dismissed as communalism. The political aspirations of eastern Bengal's Muslims, she suggests, were not adequately accommodated within the anti-partition movement.Tagore's detractors have long claimed that he opposed the establishment of Dhaka University, founded in 1921. A widely circulated allegation places him at a protest meeting in Calcutta on March 28, 1912. An investigation published by bdnews24 found that he was then at Shilaidaha, recuperating from illness, and wrote from there that day to educator Jagadananda Roy describing his health.Bangladeshi novelist and short-story writer Mozaffar Hossain recalls encountering an extraordinary rumour while growing up in the 1990s: that Tagore had secretly fed Kazi Nazrul Islam a poisonous fruit to drive him insane, supposedly to eliminate a literary rival and secure the Nobel Prize. The chronology alone demolishes the claim. Tagore won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913. Nazrul's first published poem, Mukti, appeared in 1919.Hossain sees such stories as examples of how communal prejudice can survive despite readily verifiable facts. "The language of hatred does not follow logic," he told TOI, arguing that hostility towards Tagore has often been shaped less by engagement with his writing than by attempts to set him against Nazrul.When Pakistan tried to silence TagoreAfter 1947, East Bengal became part of Pakistan, a state whose national identity was founded principally on religion. Its eastern wing, however, shared its language and much of its literary inheritance with West Bengal. In a 2008 study, scholar Anisuzzaman documents how sections of East Pakistan's intellectual establishment questioned Tagore's place in the new country's culture. In 1951, poet and scholar Syed Ali Ahsan argued for a literary identity consistent with Pakistan's Muslim character, even if that meant rejecting Tagore.Opposition was not limited to religious conservatives. Some Marxist intellectuals also criticised Tagore as bourgeois and insufficiently revolutionary. After the Bengali Language Movement of 1952, the poet's music and literature increasingly became symbols of the cultural inheritance that Bengali-speaking Pakistanis sought to preserve. His birth centenary in 1961 was celebrated despite official resistance. Those celebrations helped give rise to Chhayanaut, now one of Bangladesh's best-known cultural institutions.On June 22, 1967, information and broadcasting minister Khawaja Shahabuddin announced that songs considered inconsistent with Pakistan's cultural ideology would not be broadcasted, while the airing of other Tagore compositions would be reduced. The decision exposed divisions among East Pakistan's intellectuals over whether Tagore was indispensable to their cultural identity.Hossain points to this episode as evidence that hostility towards Tagore did not begin with the latest political upheaval. He argues that communal prejudice has long influenced cultural debates in the region."It is not new, but it has now taken a more organised form," he says. In his assessment, political and religious antagonisms have increasingly entered artistic and literary spaces, making it harder to discuss cultural figures on the merits of their work.In 1968, Anisuzzaman edited Rabindranath, an anthology of 30 essays by East Pakistani writers and scholars. Zainul Abedin drew Tagore's portrait for the book. The connection with the latest incident is striking. The same artist who drew Tagore's portrait amid the 1967 controversy was among the cultural figures depicted alongside him on the vandalised Dhaka wall. In a 2025 paper in Ethnomusicology Forum, Sahana Bajpaie argues that performing Rabindra Sangeet helped articulate a cultural identity that could challenge the religious framework promoted by Pakistan's rulers.Amar Sonar Bangla, written during the anti-partition movement of 1905, acquired a new political significance in East Pakistan. Filmmaker Zahir Raihan used it in his 1970 film Jibon Theke Neya, a satire widely understood as a critique of Pakistan's political order. The song was performed at the swearing-in of Bangladesh's provisional government on April 17, 1971, and became the national anthem after independence. Article 4 of the Constitution recognises its first ten lines as the anthem.Turmoil in Bangladesh over TagoreIn a January 2026 paper in the International Journal of Asian Studies, Mohammad A Quayum describes Bangladesh's politics as a recurring contest between ethnolinguistic and religious nationalism. Tagore has repeatedly been drawn into it. In 1979, during President Ziaur Rahman's rule, Prime Minister Shah Azizur Rahman reportedly wrote to the Cabinet Division suggesting that the anthem be replaced with Prothom Bangladesh, Amar Shesh Bangladesh. Debates over the anthem have resurfaced in subsequent decades, including after the political upheaval of 2024.Not all of Tagore's critics have argued from religion. Anisuzzaman records how Ahmed Sharif, a prominent secular intellectual, criticised Tagore in the 1980s over his social position and alleged conduct as a landlord. Other scholars challenged some of those allegations for lacking documentary support. Geography also complicates the idea of Tagore as an exclusively Indian figure. Born in Calcutta in 1861, he spent substantial periods at Shilaidaha in present-day Kushtia, managing his family's estates. Nazrul, Bangladesh's national poet, was born in what is now West Bengal.Jibanananda Das, whose portrait was added on October 13, was born and raised in Barisal in present-day Bangladesh but moved to Calcutta around the time of Partition in 1947. He died there in 1954. For Rashid, the larger question is whether modern national boundaries can reasonably determine which writers belong to a country's cultural heritage."Does Tagore belong only to India? He is not the property of any single country. He belongs to Bengalis across the world," he says.The response in Dhaka to the defacementDhaka University teachers condemned the ink attack, and a group of 37 prominent citizens warned against the exploitation of religious sentiment to fuel unrest. Udichi organised a programme of music and poetry near the mural, beginning with Bangladesh's national anthem. A rickshaw puller and a passerby helped wash the black ink from Tagore's portrait.For Zahid Newaz Khan, chief executive editor of Channel i, that response says more about Bangladesh's relationship with Tagore than the actions of those who targeted the mural. "Some misguided people committed this act, but there is a political agenda behind those instigating them," he told TOI. Tagore, he argues, is deeply embedded in the country's humanistic and cultural consciousness."A few people smeared black ink on his portrait, but an ordinary rickshaw puller came forward on his own to wash it clean. That is the real Bangladesh." Khan also draws a distinction between opposition to Indian government policies and hostility towards the poet.When Rimi called Tagore Indian, she was invoking a national boundary drawn after the poet's death. He died in 1941, six years before the partition of British India and 30 years before Bangladesh emerged as an independent country.In Crisis in Civilization, written near the end of his life, Tagore had expressed a conviction that seems particularly fitting:"And yet I shall not commit the grievous sin of losing faith in Man."The rickshaw puller just validated Tagore's words.You use AI every day. articles.title: Wynonna Judd responds to Kacey Musgraves' anti-Christopher Columbus rant: 'I'm a patriot'
articles.summary: Wynonna Judd fired back at Kacey Musgraves' anti-Christopher Columbus rant, revealing she lives by a "what would Dolly Parton do" philosophy.
articles.body: Country singer Kacey Musgraves caused quite a stir earlier this week at a concert in Texas when she called Christopher Columbus "lame" and "a loser." "Obviously f--- Columbus. Literally the lamest person to probably ever exist. Like for real. What a loser," she said to an incensed crowd when discussing the national holiday this past Monday. While Musgraves' comments received both praise and backlash, one country music legend took exception to the vulgar remarks. WYNONNA JUDD CALLS OUT ROSIE O’DONNELL AFTER POLITICAL COMMENTS LEAVE COUNTRY STAR ‘IN SHOCK’ Wynonna Judd joined Tomi Lahren on her show, "Tomi Lahren is Fearless," and when the subject of Musgraves and her anti-Columbus rant was broached, Lahren's guest did not hold back. "She has the right to do that," Judd told Lahren. "But that doesn't mean it's the right thing." METALLICA FRONTMAN JAMES HETFIELD BLASTS ENTERTAINERS PUSHING POLITICAL AGENDAS AT CONCERTS The Country Music Hall of Famer was quick to point out that the last thing she wants to do is lecture any of the fans who paid money to see her. "I never hear from my fans, 'Hey, would you come out and sing 'Grandpa' and tell me what your political view is,'" Judd explained. "My job is to be an entertaining person." "My grandmother would've had a fit," she added. Judd revealed that she lives by the thought process of "what would Dolly [Parton] do" when it comes to keeping her beliefs to herself. Much like Parton, Judd lets her actions speak louder than her words, and one of the causes closest to her heart is helping military service members. When people take her love for our troops and try to tie it to a certain political belief, the country music star says it hurts her. COUNTRY STAR CHRIS JANSON SAYS RESPECTING THE FLAG IS THE NUMBER ONE LESSON HE WANTS HIS KIDS TO LEARN "I didn't come here to talk about politics, I came to talk about music," she said. "It's nobody's business what I try to do in my private life." Despite her reticence to discuss political matters on stage, Judd wants to make one thing clear. GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU' "I'm a patriot," she proudly exclaimed. "I support my servicemen. My son is a deputy. And I am for America. Period." Judd told Lahren that when she's on stage, she goes straight to the flag, reasoning that her love of country outweighs any political belief she — or anyone, for that matter — holds. articles.title: In the 2010s, Lucky Dog host Brandon McMillan established a ranch near Los Angeles to rehabilitate shelter dogs judged “unadoptable”; his TV format placed 22 dogs in homes in 22 weeks
articles.summary: Discover how Brandon McMillan's Lucky Dog Ranch rehabilitates unadoptable shelter dogs and finds them loving homes through expert training and care, showcased in a heartwarming 22 dogs in 22 weeks television series.
articles.body: Brandon McMillan, host of the CBS series Lucky Dog, built his television career on one idea: shelter dogs labelled unadoptable can often be trained and matched with the right family. In 2010, he opened a boarding and training facility near Los Angeles that became known as the Lucky Dog Ranch. In 2013, he took the idea to American television. A format was built around training rescue dogs that shelters had given up on and matching each dog to an appropriate family.That’s where dog trainer Brandon McMillan established his reputation. In 2010, he created a boarding and training facility near Los Angeles that became known as the Lucky Dog Ranch. Its current website, Canine Minded, still peddles the idea of a boutique dog retreat where animals of any breed and temperament receive adequate training. A couple of years after the ranch opened, McMillan brought the same concept to American television. The principle could be summed up in one phrase. Train rescue dogs that shelters had given up on, and match each dog to an appropriate family.From film sets to refugeMcMillan didn’t come to shelter rescue from the usual direction. He grew up in the animal entertainment industry, and before working with dogs he trained wild animals for film and television, including lions and tigers. When his show premiered in autumn 2013, the Associated Press reported that he had trained as many as 10,000 dogs for television, films, commercials, videos and private owners. The CBS station in San Francisco described his methodology as a hybrid system that takes what he learned from wild animal training and applies it to ordinary home dogs.22 dogs in 22 weeks challengeThe series was created by Litton Entertainment, which wanted a trainer able to rescue 22 dogs, train them and place them in homes within 22 weeks, a production goal for a single season. That works out to nearly a dog a week for the whole first season. Reports at the time, including coverage in The Christian Science Monitor, said McMillan would tour animal shelters around the country, choose untrained or unadoptable dogs and bring them back to the Lucky Dog Ranch in Southern California.Training was a fixed menu. The seven commands the dogs were to learn were sit, stay, down, come, off, heel and no. McMillan would get emails from families looking for a dog, inspect the house and yard where the animal would live, and spend a couple of hours training the family before placing the dog. That step reflects an understanding that even a perfectly trained dog can fail if the home is unsuitable.One editorial decision sticks out. McMillan told the Associated Press that he could typically tell within seconds whether a dog had been abused. Those dogs are a passion for him away from the cameras, he said, but they would not appear on the show, which was aimed at viewers between 13 and 16 years old, because he felt that audience would not want to see a dog that had been in a fight. So the dogs on screen were hard cases, but some of the hardest were left to the work he did away from the cameras.Awards and the larger lessonAccording to Paramount’s press site, the series won a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Special Class Series in 2016. McMillan won his second Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Host in 2018. Lucky Dog ran for more than a decade, with McMillan hosting its first seven seasons before returning for the reunion-themed eleventh season in 2023, a long run for a show built around training rescue dogs.The 22-dog number says nothing about how many dogs are sitting in shelters around the country, and television naturally shows the success stories. What the show captures is a lesson some adopters can apply: a dog that has never been taught the basics is often labelled unadoptable, and training plus a well-chosen family can sometimes close that gap. articles.title: 9 ex-FBI employees sue Trump admin over Mar-a-Lago probe, claim political retaliation
articles.summary: Nine ex-FBI employees have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration claiming they were unlawfully dismissed due to their work on the Mar-a-Lago investigation. This lawsuit highlights alleged political motivations behind their terminations.
articles.body: Nine former FBI employees have sued the Trump administration, seeking reinstatement after being dismissed over their involvement in the investigation into Donald Trump’s handling of classified documents at his Florida estate. They allege their removal was politically motivated and violated their legal rights.The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington on Thursday, names agents, intelligence analysts and staff operations specialists who were dismissed in February. The plaintiffs say they were targeted despite carrying out assigned duties and following established law enforcement procedures.Their case adds to a series of legal challenges brought by former FBI employees dismissed under Director Kash Patel after working on investigations involving Trump or matters viewed as contrary to his administration’s interests.The nine employees deny Patel’s assertion that those dismissed had “weaponized” the bureau. Their combined experience spans more than 100 years and includes work on the Boston Marathon bombing, hostage recoveries and the 2024 assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.Their lawyers, Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio, said the dismissals punished employees for performing their duties without political bias.“In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did to follow the facts and law without bias or favor,” the lawyers said in a statement. “To this administration, this is an offense. To the rest of us, it is heroic,” as cited by AP.The lawsuit seeks the employees’ reinstatement, back pay and a court declaration that their dismissals were unlawful. It argues that the terminations damaged national security by removing experienced personnel from the FBI.The employees say they were assigned to the classified documents investigation through their work on specialised counterintelligence and counterespionage teams, rather than volunteering for the case. They allege the administration assumed their work reflected political opposition to Trump, despite having no evidence that their personal views influenced their conduct.The investigation, known within the FBI as “Plasmic Echo”, focused on classified records Trump retained after leaving the White House in 2021. Prosecutors alleged that he stored sensitive documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, showed some to people without authorisation and obstructed efforts to recover them.An FBI search of the property in 2022 recovered classified records. The investigation led to a federal indictment in Florida charging Trump with dozens of felony counts. Trump denied wrongdoing, and the case was dismissed in 2024 by US District Judge Aileen Cannon, who ruled that special counsel Jack Smith had been unlawfully appointed by the Justice Department under the Biden administration.The lawsuit argues that the employees’ dismissals were part of a wider effort to remove FBI personnel connected to investigations involving Trump. It points to Patel’s earlier criticism of the Mar-a-Lago search, which he had described as “unlawful”, and his characterisation of participating agents as “corrupt government gangsters” before he became FBI director.The complaint also cites events shortly after Trump returned to office in January 2025, when a senior Justice Department official sought a list of FBI employees who had worked on investigations involving the president. Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll resisted the demand, which employees viewed as a possible step towards mass dismissals.The plaintiffs say further rounds of dismissals followed at the FBI and Justice Department, without the hearings, notice or disciplinary procedures they believe the law requires.“The Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President’s personal vendetta,” the lawsuit states. It adds that the employees received no notice, hearing or opportunity to appeal and that no internal investigation or disciplinary process preceded their dismissals.You use AI every day. articles.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
articles.summary: Countries along NATO’s eastern flank growing increasingly concerned about the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine.
articles.body:
Poland has scrambled its defences once again as Russian attacks overnight hit western Ukraine close to Poland’s border.

Poland’s armed forces said on Friday that they had scrambled fighter jets during the attacks and no violation of the country’s airspace was recorded.

It was just the latest such alert as Poland and other countries along NATO ’s eastern flank grow increasingly concerned over the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine as Russia appears to be accelerating its tests of regional defences. Later on Friday, Bulgaria’s defence minister said Sofia has requested help from NATO to bolster its defences.

During air attacks across Ukraine overnight, numerous strikes hit the Volyn region, cutting electricity to 370,000 people across the western district, which sits on the border with Poland. Governor Roman Romaniuk reported that two people were injured.

In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.

Private power company DTEK announced on Friday that it had implemented emergency power cuts across Kyiv due to ongoing strikes.

In Russia, officials said air defences had blocked a Ukrainian drone attack against a heating plant in the Vladimir region.

Ukraine has had significant success in attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure and its oil refineries in particular. However, that strategy has provoked anger from United States President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for pushing up global oil prices.

Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said the capital’s four airports and St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport had suspended operations.

Ukrainian attacks killed two people in the Russian-controlled ‌Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed ⁠governor said.

Concern over Russian activity near NATO territory has grown since the summer as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported numerous intrusions of drones into their airspace and waters.

That activity appears to be becoming more bellicose. In recent weeks, drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing.

Drones hit two ships off ⁠Romania’s coast this week. A hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria’s coast on Tuesday prompted Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Friday that while the evidence pointed to Russia, his government does not have proof.

Shortly afterwards, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters that Bulgaria ‌has formally asked NATO to deploy combat ⁠aircraft and ⁠antidrone systems to bolster its defences.

“We have sent letters and a request to the NATO ⁠Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, ⁠urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision,” Stoyanov said.

NATO did ⁠not immediately respond to a request for comment, the Reuters news agency reported.

Stoyanov said he plans to ⁠meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts ⁠soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.

Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium ‌on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO antidrone initiative by ‌the ‌end of October.

Romania’s president has also said that his country has asked for additional equipment.

articles.title: Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's reliance on US tech, Europe admits 'can't replace capability'
articles.summary: European Union leaders are grappling with how to reduce Ukraine’s dependence on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system after disruptions to
articles.body: European Union leaders are grappling with how to reduce Ukraine’s dependence on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system after disruptions to its services raised concerns about Kyiv’s reliance on US-controlled technology for battlefield operations.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe did not have an immediate alternative to the satellite network, which has become essential to Ukraine’s military communications, as leaders gathered for a summit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also in attendance."Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can't replace this capability," Kallas said before the talks.She added that the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked and needed to develop, stressing that the gaps had to be addressed "as soon as possible".The issue has gained urgency after Ukrainian officials reported restrictions and slower speeds on parts of the Starlink system this week, amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Trump’s deal involving Russian diesel.Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to refrain from attacking Russian refineries and announced a truce on energy infrastructure attacks. However, Ukraine has continued to target Russian refineries.Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government rather than his company, SpaceX.Ukraine uses Starshield, the military-grade satellite service, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.It also uses Starlink’s civilian satellite network, but not for offensive operations.European leaders call for stronger satellite capabilitiesSeveral European leaders acknowledged that building an alternative to Starlink would take time, even as the latest disruptions highlighted the need to strengthen the continent’s satellite communications capacity."Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters."It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have, but not enough. So this is strategically something we have to discuss today."Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed the issue with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday, focusing on how European countries could provide similar services in the near future.British defence minister Wes Streeting also said he had raised Starlink with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, on Thursday."It's not yet clear to us in the UK what happened, why the service interruption occurred. But I am reassured, and was reassured directly by Secretary Hegseth, that the service has been restored," Streeting told the BBC on Friday.Ukrainian officials reported slower speeds on the system on Wednesday, affecting connectivity.Some Ukrainian officials suggested Washington was behind the restrictions reported on certain Starlink internet terminals.Eutelsat shares jump as investors look to European alternativesThe disruption has renewed investor interest in European satellite operators that could help reduce reliance on SpaceX.Shares in Eutelsat, the French satellite operator that runs the OneWeb network, rose 12 per cent on Friday, taking its gains for the week to 23 per cent. Paris-listed SES, another European satellite operator, gained 6.7 per cent.The gains followed a Reuters report citing two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter, which said an order to limit Starshield services in Ukraine had come from inside the White House.Analysts said the developments had strengthened the case for European satellite operators as governments increasingly sought alternatives to US technology."The Starlink Ukrainian issue helped," Oddo BHF analyst Stéphane Beyazian said of the share price movements, according to Reuters."But more generally, shares have been done so much due to the Starlink risk — now investors are reconsidering them as the European industry will not disappear to Starlink," he added.Eutelsat operates OneWeb, a network of around 600 low-Earth orbit satellites that provides broadband connectivity to governments, airlines and telecommunications operators. Backed by the French and British governments, OneWeb is widely viewed as Europe's leading challenger to Starlink, whose much larger satellite network dominates the global low-Earth orbit broadband market.Eutelsat chief executive Jean-François Fallacher said in March that the company had sold its entire capacity in Ukraine. The company operates as a dual-use provider, with thousands of antennas active and devices capable of operating in environments affected by GPS jamming, Reuters reported.However, analysts cautioned that European systems could not immediately match Starlink's capabilities."We don’t see (Europe's IRIS² satellite project) fully replicating Starlink’s capabilities in the short term, although SES and Eutelsat can already provide complementary satellite connectivity," ING analyst Jan Frederik Slijkerman said.Ukraine’s reliance on Starlink exposes a strategic vulnerabilityStarlink has played a central role in Ukraine’s war effort since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.Ukraine’s then deputy prime minister and digital transformation minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, publicly appealed to Musk for connectivity in the early days of the invasion. The first 500 Starlink terminals arrived in Ukraine two days later, and Musk subsequently granted the Ukrainian government and military access to the network, initially free of charge.The system has enabled secure communications between Ukrainian military units and supported command, control, intelligence and surveillance operations. Its connectivity has also been particularly important to Ukraine’s extensive use of drones.However, the relationship has faced tensions over the years. In 2022, Musk refused a Ukrainian request to activate Starlink connectivity for a planned operation near Crimea, saying that doing so would make SpaceX explicitly complicit in a major act of war and risk escalating the conflict.More recently, Musk said Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the US government, with decisions on restrictions ultimately resting with the US military and the US president.The latest disruption has again drawn attention to the risks of Ukraine relying on a satellite network controlled by a private company whose military services are subject to US government decisions.For European leaders, the immediate challenge remains how to maintain Ukraine’s communications capabilities while developing alternative systems.You use AI every day. articles.title: Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
articles.summary: As the US attacks the ICC, Kuala Lumpur welcomes a leader the court’s prosecutor wants arrested.
articles.body:
On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya with a guard of honour and an official luncheon, in the military chief’s first visit since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea in the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people.

Kuala Lumpur calls this pragmatic diplomacy. In reality, it lends a middle power’s credibility to the Trump administration’s retreat from international accountability, weakening the laws and institutions smaller states rely on most.

Since May, a surge of online hate speech and misinformation has targeted the Rohingya, Malaysia’s largest refugee community. By late July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than 100 Rohingya told UNHCR that residents of their Penang village had driven them out.

The hostility ignores the facts: Malaysia’s police chief says Rohingya account for 0.02 percent of crime. Yet research by INITIATE.MY and the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found AI-generated content amplifying anti-Rohingya disinformation across Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, casting refugees as a threat and legitimising vigilante violence.

Electoral politics plays a part. After heavy losses in three state elections, and with a general election due by February 2028, Anwar’s coalition may see a hard line on Rohingya returns as a show of control, though voter disillusionment and right-wing rivals make any electoral gains uncertain.

Malaysia is not acting alone. Mongolia hosted Vladimir Putin in 2024 despite an ICC arrest warrant, and Hungary welcomed Benjamin Netanyahu in 2025 despite another. Kuala Lumpur denies this is recognition, yet Anwar says Malaysia will work towards Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN, and Min Aung Hlaing wants a seat at the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Each welcome makes the next easier and tells leaders accused of atrocities, from Netanyahu to Min Aung Hlaing, that diplomatic rehabilitation is possible without accountability.

ASEAN has tried this before. In April 2021, Min Aung Hlaing agreed to the Five-Point Consensus, then ignored it: The violence continued, the ASEAN special envoy never met Aung San Suu Kyi, and inclusive dialogue never began. The bloc’s one real lever was excluding military leaders from its summits. Myanmar Specialist, Arkar Hein, said “Welcoming him back with nothing asked in return rewards that defiance and tells Naypyidaw that time and a staged election can achieve what compromise would otherwise require. Each handshake abroad also makes the regime less willing to offer its opponents real concessions, and convinces them that only the battlefield will decide Myanmar’s future.”

Malaysia has spent decades building its credibility as a regional peacemaker, a hard-won reputation it now puts at risk. It has facilitated the Bangsamoro peace process since 2001, helping negotiate a landmark peace agreement in the southern Philippines, and has facilitated talks in southern Thailand since 2013. In November 2024, Anwar welcomed the ICC’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, saying they “should be arrested even if they are visiting other countries”. That same month, the ICC prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity targeting the Rohingya, and an Argentinian court has since issued its own.

The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice centres on the 2016-17 operations Min Aung Hlaing commanded, which killed thousands of Rohingya, included mass rapes and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. UN investigators called for him to face genocide charges. Malaysia is not a party to the Rome Statute and has no legal duty to arrest him. But its credibility as a peacemaker and on Palestine rests on applying one standard to everyone.

The returns rest on assurances no independent body can verify. UNHCR says it was not involved in the returns and had no access to verify that they were voluntary, and that safe conditions do not exist. Those returned reportedly included 27 children. Though not a party to the Refugee Convention, Malaysia is bound by the customary principle of non-refoulement, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar has warned of substantial risks.

Naypyidaw says no Rohingya are involved because it does not recognise them as citizens, but other returnees also risk arbitrary detention, prosecution and forced recruitment. The military does not even control Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army holds more than 90 percent of the territory. On September 28, a day before returns began, a military air attack reportedly killed at least 50 civilians there, following more than a dozen other mass killings by the military earlier this year.

Nor can the military-backed government deliver the peace that safe return requires. Its election saw no voting in 67 of 330 townships, and when Min Aung Hlaing offered peace talks in April , the National Unity Government (NUG) and major ethnic armed groups refused. Without a ceasefire and an inclusive political process, assurances of safe return ring hollow.

Malaysia’s frustration is nonetheless legitimate. It has hosted refugees for decades with little international support, and resettlement has shrunk since the Trump administration suspended United States refugee admissions in January 2025. But failed burden-sharing cannot justify returns without safeguards.

The ICC exists so that victims of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can find justice when their own states fail them. That mission now faces unprecedented pressure. On October 9, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, the Trump administration sanctioned the court itself . Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad and Venezuela have announced their withdrawal.

Yet middle powers can push back. Seventy-nine ICC members, including Canada, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, backed the court after the first US sanctions in February 2025, and in May Hungary’s new government reversed its predecessor’s withdrawal. In Southeast Asia, the Philippines surrendered former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, and on October 8 judges found him fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity, with proceedings due to begin on November 30.

Middle powers like Malaysia, and blocs such as ASEAN and the European Union, cannot stop US sanctions, but they need not follow the Trump administration’s lead. As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the World Economic Forum in January, middle powers “must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”.

Malaysia and its neighbours should lead by saying no: No to efforts to weaken the court, no to treating Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency as a clean slate, and no to Rohingya returns into an active conflict. Malaysia should back efforts to hold him accountable if ICC judges issue a warrant, and reconsider acceding to the Rome Statute, a move it abandoned in 2019.

Saying no does not mean disengaging. Kuala Lumpur should tie Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN to real progress on the Five-Point Consensus, starting with an end to violence and inclusive dialogue involving the NUG and ethnic armed organisations. At home, it should pause returns until an independent body confirms they are safe and voluntary, and hold accountable those who evict, threaten or attack refugees.

Malaysia should not carry this burden alone. ASEAN partners, members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and donors should fund refugee registration, education and integration, and resettlement countries should restore their commitments. Governments should also hold tech platforms accountable for amplifying anti-refugee disinformation and require swift action against incitement.

For years, Malaysia has offered refuge to the Rohingya and others fleeing Myanmar when few countries would. That record gives it the standing, and the responsibility, to defend the system of international justice it has long championed.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: US teen accused of plotting mass shooting at Hindu temple; Indian groups mull joint action
articles.summary: Indian-origin groups in the US are considering joint action involving migrants from different backgrounds, including Punjabis and South Indians, amid
articles.body: Indian-origin groups in the US are considering joint action involving migrants from different backgrounds, including Punjabis and South Indians, amid growing concerns over alleged anti-Indian hostility following a foiled mass-shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple in Aurora, near Chicago. A 19-year-old man has been charged in connection with the alleged threat, which was reported to authorities by a co-worker.According to reports Alexandros Paporakis of Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday facing charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a weapon. According to investigators, he allegedly sent a message about the planned attack to a co-worker on Sunday, who alerted the authorities.Reports suggest that Palatine police chief William Nord said a co-worker’s tip about “concerning electronic communications” alerted authorities to the alleged plot. Police reportedly found writings expressing white supremacist views and hatred towards non-white people. Paporakis’s vehicle was also seen at an Aurora Hindu temple on Sunday. The allegations are yet to be proven in court.The incident has drawn condemnation from Indian-American organisations, which have called for a thorough investigation and action against those responsible.Sam Pitroda, former adviser to late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi who lives in the US, said the incident reflected the need to counter hatred and division with greater respect for diversity and inclusion.“The world is at a crossroads with old ideas and old institutions. We need a redesign that looks at the reality of inclusion, sustainability, AI and a lifetime opportunity to take humanity to the next level,” he said.Sam said growing political polarisation, attacks on democratic institutions and the undermining of civil society were contributing to division, fear and hostility towards people who were different.Himmat Singh, coordinator of the Sikh Coordination Committee East Coast, also condemned the reported plot and appreciated law enforcement's efforts to prevent a possible tragedy. He expressed concern over hostility towards immigrants, saying political disagreements should not become a justification for hatred against entire communities.The Indian Overseas Congress USA (IOCUSA) strongly condemned the alleged plot. Its vice-chairman George Abraham , in an official statement, said targeting a place of worship because of its religious identity would strike at the principles of religious liberty and human dignity. He called for a thorough investigation and urged authorities to bring those responsible to justice.George said that Indian Americans are a hardworking, peaceful, law-abiding community that has contributed enormously to the economic, scientific, educational, and cultural advancement of the United States. Religious freedom and respect for diverse faiths are integral parts of their heritage. No community should ever have to live in fear simply because of its ethnicity, religious beliefs, or place of worship.Meanwhile, Satnam Singh Chahal, executive director of the North American Punjabi Association (NAPA), called for Indian migrants, irrespective of their regional backgrounds, to jointly address concerns over hostility towards the community.“This is very unfortunate, but it seems to me that this action is against Indians and is a hate crime. New voices are being raised against Indians, and this teenage boy's action is proof of this,” Chahal said, referring to earlier incidents of anti-Indian rhetoric in Houston, Texas.Chahal said the association was considering convening a meeting of migrants from different backgrounds, including Punjabis and South Indians, to discuss the issue and explore a coordinated response.You use AI every day. articles.title: 16-year-old Pennsylvania student collected 60 backpacks filled with supplies and hundreds of stationery items; then distributed them across seven schools and created four ‘Kindness Karts’ to encourage students to pay kindness forward
articles.summary: A 16-year-old student from Pennsylvania, Annie McIntyre, turned an idea to help children prepare for school into a community initiative that reached seven
articles.body: A 16-year-old student from Pennsylvania, Annie McIntyre, turned an idea to help children prepare for school into a community initiative that reached seven schools across three school districts. Through a project called Build-a-Backpack, the Scranton Preparatory School student collected 60 backpacks filled with school supplies, along with hundreds of additional stationery items. She also created four “Kindness Karts”, stocked with supplies that students could take after performing an act of kindness, encouraging them to help others in return. The initiative grew through contributions from family, friends, local businesses and restaurants. What began as a school-supply drive also inspired other students to seek McIntyre’s advice on starting their own community-service projects, extending the impact of her efforts beyond the backpacks themselves.How Build-a-Backpack grew from an idea into a community projectMcIntyre developed the idea for Build-a-Backpack in March 2026, with help from her teacher, Dominique Preate. She began seeking donations in June, using social media to spread the word and placing collection boxes at local businesses and restaurants. Family members, friends and other community supporters contributed money and supplies. The collection included pencils, pens, notebooks, highlighters, crayons, erasers, glue sticks, sharpeners, scissors, rulers and markers. McIntyre organised and labelled the backpacks with supplies suited to different age groups and genders, ensuring the donations were prepared for the children who would receive them. Her project eventually reached elementary and middle schools in the Dunmore, Riverside and Scranton school districts in Lackawanna County.Four ‘Kindness Karts’ encouraged students to help othersBeyond the backpacks, McIntyre created four “Kindness Karts” stocked with school supplies that students could take after completing an act of kindness. The idea encouraged children to help someone else and continue the cycle of generosity. The project therefore combined practical assistance with a message about community responsibility. Rather than limiting the initiative to distributing supplies, McIntyre created a way for the recipients to participate in spreading kindness themselves. The karts were placed as part of the wider effort to support students and encourage positive actions within their school communities.Why the student wanted to help children prepare for schoolMcIntyre’s motivation was rooted in her appreciation for education and her wish to help younger students feel prepared to learn. Her mother, Kirsten McIntyre, told WVIA that schoolwork gave her daughter a sense of control when other parts of life felt uncertain. Annie wanted children to have the supplies they needed so they could concentrate on learning, particularly during the challenges of middle school. Lisa Owens, principal of Charles Sumner Elementary School in Scranton, praised the thought that had gone into preparing the backpacks and said pupils were excited to receive them. She also noted that the donations provided useful supplies while showing children that people in their community cared about their success.The project inspired other students to start helpingAccording to WVIA, Build-a-Backpack was McIntyre’s first major independent service project, although her mother said she had previously asked her parents to help send pizzas to nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic. McIntyre was also involved in school activities, including soccer, lacrosse and several clubs. After the backpack project, she began considering another initiative focused on summer-safety supplies, such as sunscreen. Her mother also said other students had approached Annie for advice on organising their own community-service projects. The response suggested that the initiative’s impact extended beyond the supplies distributed to schools, encouraging other young people to consider how they could contribute to their communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Istanbul’s worst floods in 80 years leave 4 dead
articles.summary: Catastrophic flooding in Istanbul was the worst in more than 80 years, Turkey’s interior minister said Friday as the death toll rose to four.
articles.body: Catastrophic flooding in Istanbul was the worst in more than 80 years, Turkey’s interior minister said Friday as the death toll rose to four. Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city with 16 million residents, was hit by more rain in the 48 hours up to Thursday morning than the combined historical average for September and October, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported. “We are trying our best to help our citizens, but we are also experiencing the biggest flood disaster since 1942,” Mustafa Ciftci said during a visit to one of the areas hit hardest by Wednesday night’s downpour. The body of a 66-year-old man was found Friday under a bridge in Istanbul’s Sariyer district. Three other deaths were previously reported, including a teenager who was electrocuted in the storm. Homes and businesses were flooded as water covered streets and parks across the city. Vehicles were washed away and many ended up piled up at the bottom of hills. Before the discovery of the body on Friday, Ciftci told reporters in Sariyer’s Ayazaga neighborhood that four people remained missing. He said there were 9,850 reports of damage and other issues related to the floods and that 46,000 personnel were working to clean up debris and help residents in Istanbul. Murat Kurum, the minister for the environment, urbanization and climate change, accompanied Ciftci to the flood-hit neighborhood. Addressing concerns that the floods were exacerbated by urban development close to waterways, he said that dealing with the problem was “essential.” Kurum, who will chair the U.N. climate change conference, COP31, next month in the Turkish city of Antalya, also linked the floods to the effects of climate change. “Combating climate change is not a choice, but a necessity,” he said.

articles.title: Archaeologists uncover unexpected twist in shipwreck mystery after clues don't add up
articles.summary: A recent nor'easter exposed a historic shipwreck on Nantucket's shore, but archaeologists say the wreckage isn't the Warren Sawyer schooner as they originally thought.
articles.body: Archaeologists thought they had identified a historic shipwreck along the Massachusetts coast — but a closer look revealed a new mystery. In late September, the remains of a historic shipwreck captured national attention after a powerful nor'easter exposed weathered wooden beams along the shore of Nantucket. At the time, officials suspected the wreckage belonged to the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted schooner that sank in 1884 and whose remains had previously been documented in the same area in 2022 and 2023, according to The Associated Press. HAUNTING CLUES EMERGE IN 7-YEAR FISHING BOAT MYSTERY AFTER WRECKAGE FOUND OFF ISLAND The ship was carrying 1,115 bales of cotton and 28 tons of scrap iron from New Orleans to Boston when it ran aground on Dec. 22, 1884, according to the Massachusetts Board of Underwater Archaeological Resources (BUAR). The captain and seven crew members were rescued, and Nantucket residents spent two weeks recovering hundreds of bales of cotton. Another storm eventually tore the vessel apart. But over 140 years later, a new discovery complicated the story when officials announced last week that the wreckage did not match previously discovered remains of the Warren Sawyer. UNDERWATER ROBOTICS EXPERT REVEALS 'SHIPWRECK CITY' HIDING BENEATH MAJOR URBAN LAKE In an Oct. 8 news release, the Egan Maritime Institute said archaeologists determined that the wreckage did not match remains of the Warren Sawyer found nearby in 2022 and 2023. Instead, following an Oct. 7 assessment, state archaeologists determined the remains appear to be a 50-foot-long section of a large merchant vessel dating to the late 19th or early 20th century. The vessel's identity remains unknown, and researchers are now turning to historical records in the hopes of identifying the ship. David Robinson, director and chief archaeologist of the BUAR, told Fox News Digital that several clues led him to question the wreckage's original identification. HAUNTING NEW IMAGES REVEAL THE FINAL SHIP WHERE EXPLORER SIR ERNEST SHACKLETON DIED During his examination, Robinson noticed the ship's wooden ribs were larger than those found in the previously documented remains of the Warren Sawyer. He also found differences in the types of wood used to construct the vessels, along with iron fastenings that appeared to date to after the Warren Sawyer sank in 1884. "Each of these shipwrecks that we see has a story to tell." "So those clues led us to believe that this probably was not from the same vessel and not Warren Sawyer," Robinson said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The wreckage may have come from a schooner barge, a type of merchant vessel commonly used to transport cargo along the East Coast during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Robinson said. Although shipwreck remains regularly emerge along the Massachusetts coastline, Robinson said the size of the newly discovered fragment makes it unusual. "What's more unusual is for those remains to be a large piece of wreckage like the 50-by-11-foot piece of the side of a ship's hull we saw recently exposed on Nantucket," he said. "This particular vessel might not be a schooner barge as it would be more likely that schooner barges would be towed through Nantucket Sound rather than the open ocean south of the island," he said. "About the best we can hope for is to maybe narrow down a list of possible candidates and apply a weight of evidence approach to see what conclusions can be drawn from the available historical and archaeological evidence."
