articles.title: Street Fighter cast say movie 'for the fans' - will they show up?
articles.summary: Cast members Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji and Callina Liang discuss the latest video game adaptation.
articles.body:
Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.

First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series.

The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987.

Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before.

But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same.

The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji.

The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour.

Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison.

The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs.

"It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat.

"And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game."

He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail.

Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film.

His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look.

"I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says.

"My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'".

Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far.

Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula.

"I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says.

"I think we could feel it when we first read the script."

Critics, though, haven't been convinced.

The Guardian called it a "garish and incoherent mess", but praised Liang as "formidable" and complimented her "genuinely impressive" fight scenes.

Gaming website IGN described the film as getting off to a "stylish start", but said it "increasingly feels disconnected from any sense of reality, even its own" along the way.

There was almost universal criticism of the "confusing" and "chaotic" plot, but some reviewers did praise the fight choreography and visuals of the film.

It's a contrast to Resident Evil, released last month, which was almost universally praised by critics and hit $300m at the global box office four weeks after release.

But will fans show up for Street Fighter?

Tayyib Mahmood, who uploads film and video game reviews to his tsreeltalk accounts, says he enjoyed Street Fighter.

"I think that it was true to what the games are," he says.

"It's taking these characters and putting them into these costumes which are unrealistic, it embraces how ridiculous these games are.

"You've got the different fighting styles, you've got these larger-than-life characters and I think the movie commits to all of that and I think there is a lot of personality to this film."

Mahmood says he has criticisms of the film, such as a weak story, but thinks the attention to the "visual identity" of Street Fighter is impressive.

He also points out that fandoms of specific video games don't always agree on what would make a good adaptation.

"I don't think that every movie needs to be loved universally," he says.

"I think that sometimes a film knows exactly who it's for and I think it does need to commit to audiences and accept that other people might hate it."

articles.title: Dublin: Children taken to hospital over chemical fumes at swimming pool
articles.summary: A dozen children and one adult were taken to hospital from the Clayton Hotel Liffey Valley on Thursday.
articles.body:
A dozen children taking swimming lessons in a Dublin pool needed medical attention after the area was contaminated by toxic fumes.

The young people and one adult were taken to hospital from the Clayton Hotel Liffey Valley on Thursday.

Irish national broadcaster RTÉ reported that a number of children were found to be suffering "respiratory distress and irritation".

The Dublin Fire Brigade (DFB)'s chief fire officer Greg O'Dwyer told RTÉ the incident was caused by "overmixing" of chlorine and another chemical in the pool's plant room.

"There were swimming lessons with 24 children in the pool at the time and some parents," he added.

He said firefighters wearing "gas-tight suits" entered the scene and "isolated the chemical".

The hotel declined to comment when contacted by BBC News NI.

In a statement, DFB said units were sent from across Dublin City, including from Tallaght, Dolphins Barn, Donnybrook and Dun Laoghaire fire stations.

"Specialist HazMat appliances from Donnybrook and Dun Laoghaire fire stations" attended and "set up a decontamination zone", they said, adding there was no danger to the wider public.

articles.title: Man jailed for burglary at snooker star Kyren Wilson's home in Northamptonshire
articles.summary: A burglar is sentenced after cash destined for a children's cancer charity is taken from Kyren Wilson.
articles.body:
A man has been jailed after he admitted burgling the home of former world snooker champion Kyren Wilson.

High-value jewellery, luxury watches, designer handbags and cash destined for a children's cancer charity were taken from his house near Kettering on 22 June, according to Northamptonshire Police.

Kane Lee, 28, of Albert Road, Luton, had initially denied the charge of burglary, but changed his plea to guilty at a hearing at Northampton Crown Court.

He was jailed for four years and ordered to pay a surcharge of £228 at a sentencing hearing earlier this week.

According to police, Lee acquired tools and clothing from B&Q and Tesco for the burglary, before driving from Luton to Kettering in a vehicle fitted with cloned number plates.

The force said he arrived after 11:00 BST and smashed the upstairs window of the four-bedroom detached house in Barton Seagrave to gain access to the property, which was unoccupied at the time.

After the burglary, Wilson said "£2,000 in cash that had been set aside as a donation to the BeMoreFab Children's Cancer Charity" had been stolen.

Wilson, who won the world title in Sheffield in 2024 , hosted an exhibition event in Corby earlier this month to raise money for the same charity.

Det Insp Alan Rooney said: "People often underestimate how violating it can feel to know that someone has been inside your home with the sole intent of stealing your property and we are pleased that the sentence reflects how much a crime such as this can affect someone."

articles.title: Thieves stole 30,000 bottles of wine worth $5.8 million from an Italian winery, using its own forklifts to load the loot onto two trucks
articles.summary: Thieves reportedly stole around 30,000 bottles of premium wine worth approximately €5 million ($5.8 million) from one of Italy’s most prestigious wine
articles.body: Thieves reportedly stole around 30,000 bottles of premium wine worth approximately €5 million ($5.8 million) from one of Italy’s most prestigious wine producers, Marchesi Antinori, in an overnight heist in Tuscany. The gang allegedly disabled security systems before using the winery’s own forklifts to load the bottles onto two trucks and escape. The theft took place at a logistics facility near Cortona, with the loss discovered by employees on October 5, 2026. The stolen shipment reportedly included the 2023 vintages of three celebrated wines: Solaia, Tignanello and Guado al Tasso. Investigators are examining how the thieves carried out the operation and whether they had advance information about the shipment.How the thieves pulled off the heistThe theft reportedly took place during the night of October 3–4 at a facility associated with Marchesi Antinori near Cortona, in Italy’s Tuscany region. According to media reports, at least seven masked individuals entered the premises and disabled security measures before beginning the operation.Rather than bringing their own loading equipment, the thieves allegedly used forklifts belonging to the winery to move the bottles onto two trucks. The operation reportedly lasted around three hours, suggesting that the group had planned how to transport the large quantity of wine.Employees discovered the missing stock when they arrived at the facility on Monday, October 5. The company subsequently coordinated with investigators before the incident became public several days later.Which wines were stolen?The stolen shipment reportedly contained approximately 30,000 bottles from three premium labels produced by the Antinori wine group. All three are associated with the 2023 vintage and have established reputations among wine enthusiasts and collectors.Solaia: A flagship wine produced at Antinori’s Tignanello estate, known for its blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Sangiovese and Cabernet Franc.Tignanello: One of the wines credited with helping establish the Super Tuscan movement, combining Sangiovese with international grape varieties.Guado al Tasso: A prestigious red wine produced at Antinori’s estate in Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast, using varieties including Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc.Reports have put the quantities of the individual labels at roughly 10,000 bottles each, although precise breakdowns should be treated cautiously where estimates differ.What are Super Tuscans?Super Tuscans are premium wines that emerged when some Tuscan producers began experimenting beyond traditional Italian wine-production rules, particularly those governing grape varieties and blends. Many combine Sangiovese, Tuscany’s signature red grape, with international varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot.These wines helped reshape the international image of Italian winemaking, gaining recognition for their quality, distinctive styles and ageing potential. Solaia and Tignanello are among the best-known names associated with the movement, while Guado al Tasso is celebrated for its connection to Bolgheri’s Cabernet-based reds.The three labels targeted in the theft are among Antinori’s recognised premium offerings, making the shipment valuable not only because of its size but also because of the wines’ established position in the market.Investigators examine how the operation was plannedThe reported disabling of security systems and the use of the winery’s own equipment have raised questions about how the thieves prepared for the raid. Italian media reports said investigators were examining surveillance footage from potential escape routes and considering whether the operation had been commissioned by a buyer.The fact that the stolen bottles were reportedly prepared for export has also drawn attention to the possibility that the thieves knew which stock would be available and when. However, the available reporting does not establish that an employee was involved or confirm that the theft was carried out on behalf of a specific buyer.Investigators are also examining whether the robbery could be connected to other recent wine thefts in Italy. No link between the incidents has been publicly established.Can the stolen wine be recovered?Recovering the shipment could prove difficult because premium wine can be distributed through intermediaries and sold in smaller quantities. Investigators may nevertheless be able to use surveillance footage, transport records, packaging details and information from legitimate distributors to trace the stolen stock.The wines’ recognisable labels and vintage could also help alert merchants and collectors to suspicious offers. However, identifying individual bottles may be more difficult if they do not carry unique traceable identifiers.As of October 16, 2026, the credible reports reviewed for this article did not confirm the recovery of the shipment or a confirmed arrest in connection with the heist. The final outcome will depend on the investigation and whether authorities can establish where the two trucks went after leaving the facility.Marchesi Antinori traces its winemaking history to 1385 and remains a family-run business, now in its 26th generation. The company has built an international reputation for its Tuscan wines and distributes its products across global markets.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Valid ID cards, 'impartial' reporting, basic first-aid: Press Council issues guidelines for journalists covering anti-SIR protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Press Council of India (PCI) has issued guidelines for journalists covering the ongoing protests in Delhi against the Special Intensive
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Press Council of India (PCI) has issued guidelines for journalists covering the ongoing protests in Delhi against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying the measures are aimed at "ensuring the safety of media personnel while enabling them to carry out their professional duties effectively."According to a PCI release, the council adopted the "Guidelines for Journalists Covering Protests and Demonstrations" at a meeting on Thursday.The guidelines advise journalists to carry valid identity cards issued by their organisations or accreditation from the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or the Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP), and keep them visibly displayed. They should calmly identify themselves to law enforcement personnel, maintain neutrality, avoid provoking confrontations and follow lawful instructions, particularly those issued for safety reasons.On safety, the PCI urged journalists to maintain a reasonable distance from confrontations, move cautiously through crowds and continually reassess their surroundings. It also cautioned against attaching cameras or recording equipment to police barricades, vehicles or other equipment in ways that obstruct movement or damage property.“Move carefully through crowds, taking short steps to reduce the risk of falling or being trampled. Continuously reassess your position in relation to protesters, counter-protesters, police, and other potential sources of danger,” the guidelines said.Journalists should remain alert to changes in crowd behaviour, approaching individuals, potential confrontations, shifts in crowd noise and emerging hazards. They should also identify and regularly reassess escape routes, including nearby exits, open streets, sidewalks and safe locations. In the event of smoke or tear gas, they should use visible landmarks and safe routes to leave the affected area without moving further into the crowd.The PCI also advised journalists to carry a compact safety kit containing first-aid supplies, water, snacks, a flashlight, a washcloth and eye protection. Depending on the assessed threat, they should consider wearing protective headgear and body armour. Journalists should learn basic first aid and avoid touching tear-gas canisters, flash-bang devices or smoke grenades.On coordination, the guidelines call on newsrooms to designate a point of contact to track journalists’ locations and respond to emergencies. Freelancers, meanwhile, should ensure that a trusted editor or contact knows their location, assignment plan and expected return time.For planned demonstrations, media organisations should coordinate with police and public information officers to clarify communication protocols and identify designated media staging areas.Emphasising journalistic ethics, the Council called for accurate and impartial reporting, urging journalists to distinguish verified facts from allegations and unconfirmed claims and to verify information through multiple sources. Statements from protesters, organisers, police and government authorities should be subjected to equal journalistic scrutiny, with claims clearly attributed.The guidelines also caution against publishing real-time police positions or escape routes if doing so could compromise safety. Journalists should describe observable actions rather than speculate about motives and exercise particular care when filming minors, injured people and private citizens in distress.The council stressed that equipment, live-broadcast commitments and pressure to obtain exclusive footage should never take precedence over journalists’ safety.(With ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: China asks Katie Zacharia to visit more often as press secretary says China did not have proper toilets
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia, the new press secretary of White House, made headlines on her first day at the job.
articles.body: Katie Zacharia, the new press secretary of White House, made headlines on her first day at the job. And now her interviews are generating more such headlines as one of her statements has drawn a comment from China. Zacharia spent years in China after her marriage as her husband had to shift to China for work. Zacharia too started working at a law firm in China. Speaking to conservative commentator Jack Posobiec, Zacharia said that when she returned from China, she wondered how that country was on the horizon without even proper toilets.“I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets’,” she said.The comment came as she was speaking about the perception in 2016 that China would soon overtake the United States. "We were all being told Hillary (Clinton) was going to win. The golden days or the glory days of America were over. That China was on the horizon," Zacharia said.South China Morning Post reported the reaction from the Chinese government on the toilet statement. Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said: “[We] welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity.”Zacharia worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China's biggest, in Beijing from 2011 to 2013.In China, foreign nationals can be hired by law firms but only Chinese nationals can be licensed as lawyers. Zacharia was never licensed to practise law -- not in China, not in the US. She clarified that she did not pass the bar exam in California in 2011, which was her first bar exam. After that, she never retook it as she did not intend to practise law. She worked as an adviser, which did not require her to clear the bar exam. She also clarified that she never called herself an attorney -- it was misinformation. She said she called herself a lawyer as advised by experts in the profession who told her that she could call herself a lawyer.Zacharia could be returning to China as early as next month when President Donald Trump is expected to take part in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern city of Shenzhen.You use AI every day. articles.title: How UN chief Antonio Guterres tests the limits of quiet diplomacy
articles.summary: Portugal’s ex-PM seeks to resolve crises via patient negotiation, but success relies on leaders’ willingness to act.
articles.body:
Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres called President Bill Clinton from Lisbon on August 30 and September 8, 1999, to discuss the growing crisis in East Timor. The small Southeast Asian territory, which had endured a brutal Indonesian occupation since 1975, was again engulfed in violence after voters overwhelmingly chose independence in a referendum. Pro-Indonesian militias responded to the vote for independence by unleashing a so-called "scorched-earth" campaign, destroying infrastructure, displacing up to half a million people and killing thousands.

The crisis resonated in Portugal, where linguistic, Catholic, and historical ties to its former colony helped fuel a solidarity movement. An estimated 10,000 demonstrators, dressed in white, formed human chains through Lisbon’s city streets.

Guterres had raised the issue before. At a 1996 summit in Bangkok, he met Indonesia’s President Suharto and broached the politically sensitive topic of East Timor, offering to restore diplomatic relations (severed since the 1975 invasion) in exchange for the release of Timorese resistance leader Xanana Gusmao. The proposal was met with an awkward silence.

This time, Guterres was asking the United States to support a UN mission in East Timor, but Washington was reluctant to confront Indonesia. Guterres recalled in his 2022 biography, “Honest Broker”, that he warned Clinton during the second call that Portugal could reconsider its Balkan deployments if the international community failed to intervene. Portugal’s contribution to NATO was small but politically well-placed, with its troops serving in the alliance’s prominent post-Cold War missions in Bosnia and Kosovo.

Guterres offered Clinton a choice: risk a public falling-out with a founding NATO ally, or use Washington’s influence to make Indonesia accept an international force in East Timor. The next day, amid growing international pressure, the White House stated that Indonesia “must” allow international assistance.

For Guterres, it was an early test of multilateral crisis diplomacy, a skill set he would later bring to his post as UN secretary-general in 2017. East Timor, also known as Timor-Leste, finally won its freedom in 2002. For spearheading diplomatic efforts during the 1999 crisis, Guterres was awarded Timorese citizenship in 2024.

“Antonio Guterres pushed a lot for what we now call the referendum, and when violence broke out he was one of the people calling for a UN intervention,” said Christine Cabasset, a teacher at Lille Catholic University and an expert on East Timor, reflecting on how the East Timor crisis foreshadowed Guterres’s later career.

“Guterres had a critical role all along the way,” she added, noting how he later pushed for the creation of the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor.

“There is also a kind of love story with the UN, I mean, that strong link between Timor-Leste and the UN… Multilateralism, which is still really the purpose of the UN, has been critical in the independence of Timor-Leste. And Guterres [himself] became very important in the UN starting from 2005.”

Guterres’s response to the East Timor crisis reflected an approach shaped by his Catholic faith, his early work with Portugal’s poor and his political coming of age after the fall of a dictatorship. He carried those experiences into a career built on finding common ground and helping people caught in crises. But as UN secretary-general, he has faced the limits of that approach, struggling to turn appeals for peace into action when the world’s most powerful countries are at odds.

articles.title: Israeli settlers continue progrom amid olive harvest in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: At least two people, including Washington Post journalist, injured as settlers armed with clubs and guns attack.
articles.body:
Masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to olive trees in the occupied West Bank, as Israeli pogroms in the territory continue.

Approximately 80 masked settlers armed with clubs charged at Palestinians in the village of Abu Falah as they picked fruit. The harvest, which provides an economic lifeline in the territory, has become a regular target of Israelis from illegal settlements, who have stepped up violence amid encouragement from the government for the expansion of settlements.

As the settlers confronted them, some using slingshots, the Palestinians responded by throwing rocks. Israeli ⁠military jeeps sped into the area, but the attack continued, and the soldiers fired tear gas in the direction of the Palestinians.

More settlers armed with machineguns then arrived, Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who was on the ground, told Al Jazeera.

The sound of live gunfire could be heard in the area, and a photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun, the Reuters news agency reported.

Describing violence in the West Bank as being “at or near an all-time high right now”, Nathaniel said everyone ran when the settlers began firing, at which point Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine fell to the ground.

“We saw that there was a journalist … on the ground [with] people beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” he said.

Levine later said she “probably wouldn’t even be here” had it not been for her helmet and flak jacket.

The attack extends the increasingly frequent pogroms carried out by settlers as Israel’s government pushes to expand its illegal settlements on Palestinian land.

Last month, Amnesty International said Israel had signed at least 15 land confiscation orders covering approximately 200 dunams (20 hectares) of Palestinian land in Jenin, in the northern West Bank. The rights group said it appeared Israel intended to connect two planned settlements in the area.

The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), an independent conflict-monitoring organisation, said recently that settler violence in the West Bank has reached record levels.

The growing violence and Israel’s expansionist policies have come under intense scrutiny in recent months, with allies including the UK and France announcing sanctions targeting the purchase of goods from illegal settlements.

The policy change marks a dramatic shift in stance by Western countries, which had previously refrained from going beyond verbal criticism of Israel’s actions.

articles.title: Israeli settlers burn olive trees, injure journalist in West Bank attack
articles.summary: Clad in black and their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on Friday on an occupied West Bank village’s annual harvest that injured at least two people including a journalist.
articles.body: Clad in black and their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on Friday on an occupied West Bank village’s annual harvest that injured at least two people including a journalist. Some 80 settlers, some of them carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill above a terraced olive grove where villagers from Abu Falah had gathered to pick ripe fruit, a cherished annual tradition in Palestinian life, Reuters witnesses said. The settlers took positions in front of the terraced lanes of olive trees. Some of them used slings to launch rocks towards Palestinian villagers, who descended towards the bottom of the hill before picking up and throwing stones to defend themselves. “The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the attack in Abu Falah. Partway through the attack, at least two Israeli military jeeps sped through the area, kicking up dust as villagers ran out of their way. The attack continued after the military’s arrival, with Israeli soldiers firing tear gas in the direction of the Palestinians who had dodged the jeeps. The sound of live gunfire could be heard in the area, and a Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Palestinian medics said two people were injured and taken to hospitals in the area of Ramallah. One of them was Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post. Video of the attack showed Levine lying on her side on a dirt path with her hands over her face as at least three settlers surrounded her. Speaking from a hospital bed later, Levine, who is in stable condition, said: “I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me.” Levine said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened, after which medics rushed her in an ambulance to a clinic in Abu Falah and then to hospital in Ramallah. Her voice shook as she spoke and she had bandages over her left hand. The Washington Post did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has surged, with at least 170 attacks since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group. The settlers have been emboldened by the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has overseen a rapid expansion of settlements and smaller outposts across the West Bank. Netanyahu has criticized the violence but has taken few steps to crack down on incidents that have drawn international condemnation and sanction plans by longtime Israeli allies, including Britain. The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians. UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied. The Abu Falah attack followed a similar attack on Friday morning in the area of Turmus Ayya village, where settlers burned three cars after attacking a group of farmers harvesting olives. The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack in Turmus Ayya, said the settlers “snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him.”
